Your hourly quote applies to billable hours: plan for the rest of the working year

Four interactive charts turn leave, downtime, unpaid work and business costs into an annual pre-tax cash budget and a conditional hourly-rate requirement.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Turn an hourly quote into an annual capacity budget

Interactive planning lab

Annual billable hours1290.0
Cash remaining before personal tax$94,680
Rate needed for the entered annual target$87.63

Original hypothetical annual capacity budget for a sole operator. Exactly 52 equal weeks; leave and other downtime are non-overlapping weeks with no work. Remaining weeks have the entered hours, split between billable and unpaid work. Every billable hour is sold, invoiced and collected within this same year at the same rate. Rates exclude sales tax. Variable cash costs use collected fees; fixed business costs and a separate personal provision are counted once. Remaining cash is before personal income tax, CPP/QPP, EI and other personal liabilities. No tax deductibility, legal employment status, guaranteed demand, collection delay, corporate tax, debt, investment return or replacement of an actual employee benefit is calculated. Personal provision is a cash allocation, not a deemed business expense or tax deduction.

The central idea

A quoted hourly rate becomes annual cash only through hours you can sell and collect. Budget unpaid work and fixed costs before treating the quote as a household income rate.

01

Separate the work relationship from the pricing arithmetic

An hourly quote is a unit price, not a promise of forty paid hours every week. Before building a household budget around it, establish how many hours can produce collected fees and what those fees must fund.

Worker status is a separate question. The CRA’s Employee or Self-employed guide says the facts of the working relationship as a whole decide employment status. A chosen contract label or a favourable calculator result does not settle it. The guide also explains the option of requesting a CPP/EI ruling when status is uncertain.

This tool assumes an independently established sole-operator business arrangement. It performs annual capacity and cash-allocation arithmetic. It does not determine employment status, statutory contributions, labour-law rights, tax deductions or the value of an actual employee benefit.

02

Build the time budget before multiplying by the hourly rate

The example uses a simple fifty-two-week template, with forty hours assigned to each available workweek. Five weeks are reserved for leave and four other weeks for downtime. These categories are assumed not to overlap, leaving forty-three working weeks.

That produces 1,720 working hours. A quarter of them, or 430 hours, is assigned to work that cannot be billed: for example, administration, business development or maintaining systems. The remaining 1,290 hours are the billable capacity used by the model.

The time chart also shows 360 hours of no-work capacity. That is nine unavailable weeks multiplied by the forty-hour template; those hours are not actually worked. Billable hours, unpaid working hours and no-work capacity together reconcile to the template’s 2,080 hours.

All 1,290 billable hours are assumed to find buyers and be collected in the same year. This is a strong assumption. Time available to sell a service does not establish demand, and an invoice does not establish collection. Use the separate invoice-cash guide to test when money reaches the bank.

03

Follow collected fees through the costs they must cover

At CAD 100 per billable hour, the selected capacity generates CAD 129,000 of collected fees, excluding sales tax. Variable business cash costs take 8%, or CAD 10,320. Annual fixed business cash costs take another CAD 12,000, leaving CAD 106,680 before a separate personal allocation.

The example then assigns CAD 12,000 to a personal provision. This might represent a separately budgeted amount for protection or saving, but the tool gives it no automatic tax treatment and assumes no equivalence with employer benefits. Counting it as a cash allocation keeps it from being spent again elsewhere.

After that provision, CAD 94,680 remains before personal income tax, CPP/QPP, EI and other personal liabilities. It is not take-home pay. It includes the cash available to reward the owner’s work and bear business risk; no separate owner wage has been deducted.

BDC’s pricing overview explains the need to account for costs and overhead when examining a break-even point. The waterfall here uses a deliberately simple cash structure, rather than reproducing a formal cost-of-sales statement or claiming that every entered expense is deductible.

04

Solve for a rate only after stating the annual target

The target input asks for annual cash remaining after the entered business costs and personal provision, but before personal tax. Its default is CAD 80,000. This target is separate from the CAD 12,000 provision, so the model does not quietly count that allocation twice.

To solve for the rate, add the target, fixed business costs and provision. Divide their CAD 104,000 total by the billable hours multiplied by the 92% left after variable costs. The required rate is approximately CAD 87.63 per billable hour under these assumptions.

The line chart varies the quote and shows where annual remaining cash meets the target. A crossing above the displayed range can still produce a numeric required rate. That calculation does not make the price commercially attainable or prove that the assumed number of hours will sell.

When there are no billable hours, the tool reports that no billable hours are available rather than dividing by zero. Fixed cash costs and the chosen provision remain in the budget. They do not disappear merely because all working time becomes unpaid or every week is unavailable.

05

Use the sensitivity grid to choose what needs better evidence

The matrix changes the quote and the unpaid share together. A larger unpaid share leaves fewer hours producing fees while fixed costs continue. A higher quote raises modeled revenue only because the grid holds sold hours unchanged. It does not model customers buying fewer hours at a higher price.

Before relying on a cell, check recent time records, confirmed bookings, cancellation terms, collection experience and the costs that continue during downtime. Keep leave and other unavailable weeks distinct so the same week is not removed twice.

For household planning, add a separate assessment of personal tax, statutory contributions, protection needs and the timing of withdrawals. A full year’s positive result may still coexist with an early cash shortage. The useful output is a documented capacity budget and a set of assumptions to verify, not a salary comparison or an instruction to charge a particular rate.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Every rate, cost, time allocation and target is an original hypothetical assumption. This annual capacity illustration assumes full collection and excludes personal tax and statutory contributions. It does not classify a worker, quote a market price or establish equivalence with an employee salary or benefit plan. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. CRA · Employee or Self-employed, RC4110 ↗

    Official HTML reviewed 25 October 2026; publication marked Rev.23. Supports the facts-of-relationship boundary and the CPP/EI ruling route. This article does not apply the legal status tests or use dated contribution figures.

  2. BDC · Seven steps to setting the right price for products or services ↗

    Public primary business guidance updated 1 August 2023 and reviewed 25 October 2026 for cost, overhead and break-even context. All rates, hours and costs in the graphics are independently authored assumptions, with no market-rate dataset.
